subject: physics

moments.title: Einstein predicts gravitational waves
moments.body:
Einstein, having completed general relativity in November 1915, predicts in 1916 that accelerating masses should produce ripples in spacetime — gravitational waves — travelling at the speed of light.

The predicted amplitudes are tiny. Einstein himself is sceptical that they could ever be detected. In 1936 he writes a paper (with Nathan Rosen) arguing they don't really exist — gets it rejected by Physical Review after peer review (he had never previously been peer-reviewed and was furious) and eventually withdraws.
moments.takeaway: A core prediction of general relativity — that Einstein himself sometimes doubted — waits a century for confirmation.

moments.title: Binary pulsar PSR B1913+16
moments.who: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor, Arecibo
moments.body:
Hulse and Taylor discover a pulsar in a binary system with another neutron star. Over years of observation, they measure the orbital period shortening at a rate exactly matching the prediction of gravitational-wave emission carrying energy away from the system.

This is the first indirect detection of gravitational waves. The 1993 Nobel Prize is awarded.
moments.takeaway: Gravitational waves are real. Their energy loss can be measured indirectly through orbital decay.

moments.title: Building LIGO
moments.who: LIGO collaboration, Hanford and Livingston, USA
moments.body:
The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory consists of two L-shaped detectors, each with arms 4 km long, in Hanford (Washington) and Livingston (Louisiana). Laser light bounces between mirrors at the ends of the arms. Passing gravitational waves stretch and squeeze the arms by tiny amounts (less than 10 to the minus 18 m).

Construction starts in 1994. First operations 2002. After 13 years of upgrades and null results, Advanced LIGO begins observing on 18 September 2015.
moments.takeaway: An instrument sensitive enough to measure a fraction of a proton's diameter over 4 kilometres. The most precise length measurement humans have built.

moments.title: GW150914 — first direct detection
moments.body:
At 09:50:45 UTC on 14 September 2015 — just days after Advanced LIGO begins observation — both detectors record a chirp signal lasting 0.2 seconds. The waveform matches predicted general-relativity gravitational waves from the merger of two black holes, 36 and 29 solar masses, into a single 62 solar mass black hole, about 1.3 billion light-years away.

Three solar masses' worth of energy is radiated as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second — briefly outshining all the stars in the observable universe.

quote.text: We have detected gravitational waves. We did it.
quote.attrib: David Reitze, LIGO Executive Director, press conference 11 February 2016

moments.takeaway: Einstein's 1916 prediction is confirmed exactly 100 years later. A new astronomy begins.

moments.title: Multi-messenger astronomy: GW170817
moments.body:
On 17 August 2017, LIGO and the Virgo detector in Italy observe gravitational waves from a neutron-star merger. Within 2 seconds, the Fermi space telescope detects a short gamma-ray burst from the same direction.

Within hours, optical telescopes worldwide point at the source and observe a 'kilonova' explosion. Heavy elements (gold, platinum, uranium) are observed being created in real time by r-process nucleosynthesis. The cosmic origin of half the elements heavier than iron is identified.
moments.takeaway: Gravitational waves, gamma rays, X-rays, optical, infrared and radio observations of the same event. Multi-messenger astronomy is born.

now.title: Gravitational-wave astronomy today
now.body:
Over 90 gravitational-wave events have been detected since 2015 — mostly binary black hole mergers, some neutron star mergers, one black hole-neutron star coalescence. The catalogue is growing every observing run.

LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA (Japan) operate. Future detectors: LISA (space-based, three spacecraft in formation, ESA/NASA, planned launch 2035) and Einstein Telescope (underground, Europe).
now.open_questions: What's the maximum mass of a black hole formed by stellar collapse? Do intermediate-mass black holes exist? Are there gravitational-wave sources beyond compact binaries (e.g. cosmic strings, primordial black holes)? Can we use gravitational waves to measure cosmological parameters independently of electromagnetic methods?

reflection: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916, doubted them in 1936, and was vindicated in 2015 — 60 years after his death. How does a discipline handle the gap between prediction and verification when it spans an entire human lifetime?
